"Going-over" is an informal word with three distinct meanings. What ties them all together is the idea of doing something thoroughly — not lightly or halfway, but fully and without holding back. Understanding this core idea makes all three meanings feel natural.
Meaning 1: A thorough examination or inspection

This is the most common meaning. When you give something (or someone) a going-over, you check it carefully and completely — not a quick glance, but a proper, detailed look from start to finish.

Examples:

  • "The mechanic gave the car a thorough going-over before we agreed to buy it."
  • "The doctor gave him a complete going-over and said he was in perfect health."
  • "She gave the contract a careful going-over before signing."
  • "Before the guests arrived, she gave every room in the house a going-over."

Notice that it is nearly always used in the pattern: give [something/someone] a going-over. You can also say get a going-over, which is the same thing from the other person's perspective — "The car got a going-over before we bought it."

The object of the examination can be a thing (a document, a room, a machine) or a person (a patient, an athlete, a new recruit). In either case, the meaning is the same: examined carefully and completely.

In informal speech, "a going-over" can mean a physical attack — being beaten up badly.

Examples:

  • "A group of men gave him a going-over and left him on the ground."
  • "He looked terrible — like he'd been given a real going-over."

This meaning is less common but important to know. It almost always implies that the beating was serious, not just a light scuffle.
Meaning 3: A harsh scolding or severe criticism

"A going-over" can also mean being angrily and thoroughly told off — usually by someone in authority (a boss, a teacher, a parent, a coach).

Examples:

  • "The manager gave the whole team a going-over for missing the deadline."
  • "His father gave him a real going-over when he came home at 3 a.m."
  • "The coach gave her a going-over in front of everyone for breaking the rules."

The key idea here is that the scolding is not brief or mild — it is extended, thorough, and pointed. The person being criticized feels the full weight of it.
How to tell which meaning is intended

Context will almost always make it obvious:

  • If the subject is an object (car, house, document) or a body being medically examined → it means an examination.
  • If the setting is violent or threatening → it means a beating.
  • If someone is angry and in a position of authority → it means a scolding.

There is also a question of degree. Notice that in all three uses, people often say "a real going-over" or "a thorough going-over" to emphasize that it was especially intense. This adds force to whichever meaning is being used.
Why all three meanings feel connected

At first glance, an "examination," a "beating," and a "scolding" seem like very different things. But in all three cases, the same underlying idea is present: someone or something is being worked over completely — not spared, not handled gently, but dealt with from top to bottom, fully and forcefully. That's the spirit the word carries across all its uses.

This word is informal. It belongs in everyday conversation, not in formal writing. In professional or formal contexts, you would replace it with:

  • "Thorough examination" or "inspection" (for Meaning 1)
  • "Assault" or "attack" (for Meaning 2)
  • "Reprimand," "dressing-down," or "rebuke" (for Meaning 3)

The traditional plural is goings-over (because the main word is "going," so that's what gets pluralized — similar to how "mothers-in-law" works). In modern writing, "going-overs" is also used. In practice, though, the plural almost never comes up, because people typically say "he gave them each a going-over" rather than "he gave them two goings-over."
